key_terms.meaning: A shared secret string stored by the server only as a salted hash such as H(salt‖password), never as plaintext.
Server sends a fresh random number (nonce); client proves the secret by hashing or encrypting it with the nonce, so an old answer is useless.
Proving identity with two or more different factors: something you know, something you have, something you are.
The trusted server in Kerberos that holds a master key per user and per service and issues tickets.
A time-limited ticket encrypted under the KDC's secret key that the client shows to get service tickets.
A one-way agreement in IPsec holding the keys, algorithms, SPI and sequence numbers for one direction of traffic.
IPsec's Authentication Header (integrity plus origin, no encryption) and Encapsulating Security Payload (encryption plus integrity).
The opening exchange that agrees a cipher suite, authenticates the server by certificate and derives a shared session key.
A trusted body that signs a certificate binding a public key to a name, so a stranger's key can be trusted.
Sender Policy Framework: a DNS TXT record listing the IP addresses allowed to send mail for a domain.
DomainKeys Identified Mail: the sender signs selected headers and the body; the receiver verifies using a public key published in DNS.
A DNS policy that tells receivers what to do when SPF and DKIM both fail, and where to send reports.
Digital signatures added to DNS records so a resolver can check the answer is authentic and unmodified.
DNSSEC's signature record over a resource record set, and the parent-zone record that hashes a child zone's key.
The exchange that turns a pre-shared key or 802.1X key material into a fresh per-session pairwise key and proves both sides hold it.
Port-based access control with three roles: supplicant (device), authenticator (switch or access point) and authentication server (RADIUS).
Extensible Authentication Protocol: a carrier for authentication methods such as EAP-TLS, EAP-TTLS and PEAP.
An encrypted, authenticated envelope that carries private packets across the public Internet between two gateways or a client and a gateway.
Untrusted input reaching a query string so that data is read as code; fixed by parameterised queries and least privilege.
Untrusted input echoed into a page so a script runs in another user's browser; fixed by output encoding and CSP.

takeaways: Authentication proves an identity using a secret, a device or a body trait; a fresh challenge is what stops a recorded answer from being replayed.
Kerberos never sends a password over the network: it issues short-lived symmetric tickets from a trusted KDC, so compromise has an expiry date.
IPsec moves protection down to the network layer, so every packet gets authentication and, with ESP, encryption under a named security association.
TLS and SSH both do handshake-then-record: asymmetric work authenticates and agrees a key, symmetric keys then protect the bulk data cheaply.
SMTP has no built-in sender proof, so mail security signs at the message level (PGP, S/MIME) and adds domain-level checks (SPF, DKIM, DMARC).
DNSSEC gives integrity and authenticity of DNS answers, not confidentiality or availability, and it depends on a signed chain from the root zone down.
Wireless is an open medium, so the real job is mutual authentication plus a fresh per-session key, never a static shared key reused forever.
802.1X decides whether a device may join at all, while a VPN extends a private network securely over the public Internet.
Most web breaches come from ordinary coding faults: injection, broken access control, session theft and misconfiguration, not from broken ciphers.
bank_note: Long answers are expected to compare mechanisms side by side (Kerberos against TLS, IPsec against TLS, DNSSEC against HTTPS) and to finish with concrete defences, not just definitions.

bank.q: Define entity authentication and message authentication. Explain, with a message exchange, how a challenge-response protocol defeats a replay of an old password response.
outline: Entity authentication: proof of a live party's identity now.
Message authentication: proof that a message came from the claimed source and was not altered.
Challenge: server sends nonce; client returns hash of nonce, password and shared salt.
Replay fails because the nonce differs each run; mention time-stamping and sequence numbers as alternatives.
Contrast with sending a plaintext or even a hashed static password, which is replayable.

bank.q: Describe the Kerberos authentication exchange. Explain the roles of the KDC, the ticket-granting ticket and the service ticket, and why passwords never cross the network.
outline: KDC split into AS and TGS conceptually.
Step 1: client authenticates to AS, gets TGT encrypted under KDC key.
Step 2: client shows TGT plus an authenticator to get a service ticket.
Step 3: client presents service ticket to the application server.
Tickets carry a session key and a lifetime; the timestamp in the authenticator bounds replay.
Password is used only locally to derive a key, so it is never transmitted.

bank.q: Explain the IPsec architecture: security association, SPI, AH and ESP, transport mode and tunnel mode.
outline: SA is one-way, identified by SPI plus destination address plus protocol.
AH gives integrity and data origin authentication of the IP packet, no confidentiality.
ESP gives confidentiality plus integrity and hides inner headers in tunnel mode.
Transport mode protects payload for host-to-host; tunnel mode wraps whole packets for gateways.
IKE negotiates SAs and keys; mention anti-replay window with sequence numbers.

bank.q: Describe the TLS 1.3 handshake and the TLS record protocol. Explain how the session key is derived and what the certificate does.
outline: ClientHello with key share, cipher suites and supported groups.
ServerHello plus encrypted extensions, certificate, CertificateVerify and Finished.
Key exchange is ephemeral Diffie-Hellman; CertificateVerify signs the transcript with the server's key.
Key schedule derives handshake and application traffic keys from the shared secret.
Record layer encrypts and authenticates with AEAD; sequence numbers prevent replay and reordering.

bank.q: A bank wants to stop phishing mail that forges its domain name. Explain how you would deploy SPF, DKIM and DMARC together and what each one still fails to stop.
outline: SPF: publish allowed sending IPs in DNS; fails on forwarding because the envelope sender changes.
DKIM: sign selected headers and body hash; survives forwarding but only covers what is signed.
DMARC: alignment of From domain with SPF or DKIM, plus policy p=none/quarantine/reject and reporting addresses.
Still cannot stop lookalike domains, compromised legitimate accounts or malicious content from a valid domain.
Mention MTA-STS or TLS for transport and user training as complements.

bank.q: Design an 802.1X deployment for a campus wireless network using PEAP-MSCHAPv2, and list the steps a laptop follows before it receives an IP address.
outline: Roles: supplicant on laptop, authenticator is the access point or controller, authentication server is RADIUS.
EAPOL start, identity request and response, then TLS tunnel to the server certificate.
Inner MSCHAPv2 exchange inside the tunnel; server checks credentials against the directory.
RADIUS Access-Accept carries keying material for the wireless session; VLAN or role assigned.
Then DHCP and normal traffic; a reject puts the port in a quarantined VLAN.
Weakness: the client must verify the server certificate or it is open to an evil twin.

bank.q: Explain the SSH transport layer, user authentication and connection layers, and how SSH differs from TLS in purpose and trust model.
outline: Version exchange, key exchange, server host key proves server identity, keys derived.
User authentication: public key, password or keyboard-interactive over the encrypted channel.
Connection layer multiplexes channels, port forwarding and SFTP.
TLS uses CA-signed certificates by default; SSH uses host keys pinned in known_hosts on first contact.
TLS protects arbitrary application data; SSH is primarily remote login and tunnelling.

bank.q: Explain how PGP and S/MIME provide email confidentiality and authentication. Compare their trust models and describe the private key ring and key ID.
outline: Message encryption: random session key encrypted under the recipient's public key; message encrypted under the session key.
Signature: hash of message signed with sender's private key, optional.
PGP trust is a web of personal signatures; S/MIME uses X.509 hierarchies and CMS structures.
Private key ring stores the user's own key pairs, indexed by key ID and protected by a passphrase.
Key ID is the short fingerprint fragment used to name the key without sending the whole key.
S/MIME is built into mainstream mail clients; PGP needs add-ons.

bank.q: Compare DNSSEC and HTTPS/TLS as protections for a web lookup. Why does DNSSEC alone not give confidentiality, and what does it still leave exposed?
outline: DNSSEC signs record sets; a resolver validates a chain of trust from the root through DS and DNSKEY records.
It gives integrity and authenticity of the answer, not encryption; queries are still readable.
HTTPS protects the content and the destination name at the application layer, including confidentiality.
DNSSEC does not stop denial of service, zone enumeration without NSEC3, or a compromised authoritative server.
Both together close different gaps; mention DNS over HTTPS or TLS for privacy of queries.

bank.q: Trace the security mechanisms in play when a user opens a banking site over a cafe Wi-Fi network, from association to the first HTTP request.
outline: Association and 4-way handshake derive a fresh pairwise key; open networks give no authentication of the access point.
Captive portal or 802.1X may gate access; identity of the hotspot is unverified here.
DNS resolution, with DNSSEC validation if the resolver supports it.
TLS handshake authenticates the bank by certificate, ephemeral key exchange gives forward secrecy.
Record layer encrypts the request; HSTS prevents a plaintext first attempt.
Risks left: evil twin, malicious resolver, compromised client, and the user ignoring certificate warnings.

bank.q: WEP has been broken while WPA2 stands up to the same attacks. Explain, using the 4-way handshake, what design differences matter and what remains weak in WPA2.
outline: WEP: static shared key, 24-bit IV, RC4, weak integrity check; IV reuse leaks keystream.
WPA2: per-session pairwise key from the 4-way handshake, AES-CCMP with proper integrity.
Handshake proves both sides hold the pairwise master key without revealing it; nonces stop replay.
Remaining weaknesses: offline dictionary attack on the passphrase from a captured handshake, KRACK-class implementation flaws, no protection of management frames until 802.11w.
Conclusion: key freshness and a real integrity check are the design wins.

bank.q: A company allows split tunnelling on its VPN. Evaluate the security trade-off and state the policy controls you would add.
outline: Split tunnelling sends only corporate traffic through the tunnel; other traffic goes direct.
Benefit: less bandwidth and latency at the gateway, better user experience.
Risk: the client sits on two networks, so it can bridge malware or expose the corporate side.
Controls: endpoint posture checks, host firewall, always-on VPN for sensitive roles, DNS handling to avoid leaks.
Monitoring and logging of tunnel use; data loss prevention on the endpoint.

bank.q: Pick two OWASP-class vulnerabilities, such as injection and broken access control. Explain how each is exploited and rank the defences by how much they actually help.
outline: Injection arises when untrusted input is concatenated into a query or command, so data becomes code.
Defence ranking: parameterised queries first, then input validation as a secondary layer, then least privilege on the database account, then WAF as a last net.
Broken access control: a request for another user's object ID is served because the check is missing on the server.
Defence: server-side authorisation on every request, deny by default, unguessable identifiers are not a control.
Common ground: never trust the client, centralise the check, test with automated scans and manual review.

bank.q: Explain multi-factor authentication and describe how a FIDO-style security key or TOTP app changes the threat model compared with SMS one-time codes.
outline: Factors: knowledge, possession, inherence; MFA needs different kinds, not two of the same.
Passwords alone fall to phishing, reuse and credential-stuffing breaches.
SMS OTP is vulnerable to SIM swap, interception and real-time relay phishing.
TOTP app removes the telecom link but is still phishable in real time.
Hardware authenticator binds the response to the site origin, so a proxy phishing page gets a useless signature.

bank.q: Explain how a network access control (NAC) system combines 802.1X, posture checks and VLAN assignment, and analyse what an attacker on the inside can still do.
outline: 802.1X authenticates the device or user before the port carries traffic.
Posture check: patch level, antivirus, disk encryption before full access.
Result is a role or VLAN: full, limited or quarantine.
Insider attacker with valid credentials still passes; lateral movement needs segmentation and monitoring.
MAC authentication bypass and MAB spoofing are weak spots; mention IDS and anomaly detection.

glossary.def: A value used once, so that a fresh run of a protocol cannot be answered with a recorded old reply.
An attacker resends a captured valid message hoping the receiver acts on it again.
A random value stored with a hashed password so identical passwords hash differently and precomputed tables fail.
A short-lived symmetric key used for one connection and then discarded.
In Kerberos, a block encrypted under a server's secret key that carries the client name and a session key.
A client-name and timestamp block encrypted under the session key, proving the presenter is live.
The device that asks to join the network in 802.1X.
The switch or access point that blocks the port until the authentication server answers.
The RADIUS server that checks credentials and returns accept or reject with keying material.
Network access control: the policy system that decides whether a device may join and at what level.
A protected EAP method that builds a TLS tunnel with a server certificate and then runs an inner method inside it.
An EAP method where both client and server authenticate with certificates inside the TLS handshake.
A virtual private network: an authenticated, encrypted tunnel carrying private traffic over a public network.
A VPN setting where only selected traffic goes through the tunnel and the rest goes direct to the Internet.
Forging a sender address, name or identity so a message appears to come from someone else.
A message or site that impersonates a trusted party to make the user hand over credentials or data.
Unsolicited bulk mail, often the delivery vehicle for phishing and malware.
Cryptographic Message Syntax, the standard structure that S/MIME uses for signed and encrypted messages.
A short fingerprint fragment that names a public or private key without transmitting the whole key.
The local store of a user's own key pairs in PGP, protected by a passphrase.
A portion of the DNS namespace managed together, with its own keys when DNSSEC is used.
A rogue wireless access point using a legitimate network's name to capture traffic or credentials.
Writing past the end of a buffer, which can overwrite a return address and redirect execution.
Cross-site request forgery: a hostile page makes the victim's browser send an authenticated request.
